name: UCall (formerly ujrpc)
workload: JSON-RPC 'sum' call over a persistent TCP connection; latency measured with 1 client, throughput with 32 concurrent client processes on AWS c7g.metal (Graviton3)
claimed_speedup: UCall with io_uring (C): 22µs latency / 231,000 rps vs UCall with POSIX/epoll (C): 62µs latency / 79,000 rps -- about 2.8x lower latency and 2.9x higher throughput from switching the same codebase from epoll to io_uring; also cites up to 100x vs FastAPI over REST (3,184 rps) and vs FastAPI over WebSocket (11,356 rps)
hardware: AWS c7g.metal (Graviton3 ARM), Ubuntu 22.10, Linux kernel 5.19
tradeoffs: io_uring path requires Linux 5.19+; POSIX/epoll fallback available on older kernels; project has been renamed (ujrpc -> UCall) and appears to have slowed down; small pet-project scale (a few thousand LOC) vs mature frameworks like FastAPI/gRPC
caveats: First-party README benchmark; compiler and build flags not stated; the cleanest comparison is the internal POSIX-vs-io_uring row (same codebase); the FastAPI/gRPC rows compare across languages/stacks and are far less controlled
found_via: Hacker News: 'Show HN: Faster FastAPI with simdjson and io_uring on Linux 5.19' (https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=35042316), query 'io_uring benchmark'

name: BusterMQ
baseline: NATS Server (nats-server, Go, epoll-based via Go's netpoller)
workload: Pub/sub fan-out benchmark (examples/benchmarks:bench_pub_sub_route) with 10x fan-out, 16 server threads and 16 benchmark client threads on an AMD Ryzen 9950X
claimed_speedup: +ROUTE mode: 6.78M msg/s publish, 8.80 GB/s bandwidth, p50 latency 5.02ms vs Go NATS: 2.16M msg/s, 2.94 GB/s, p50 latency 55.70ms -- roughly 3.1x publish rate, 3x bandwidth, ~11x lower p50 latency
compiler_and_flags: Bazel 'optimized release binary' (bazel build //src:bustermq); exact compiler and flags not stated
hardware: AMD Ryzen 9950X, 16 threads for server + 16 threads for benchmark client
tradeoffs: Zig + Bazel toolchain; implements only core NATS features, not the full protocol; SQPOLL/busy-poll modes trade CPU for latency
caveats: First-party, self-run, single-host benchmark; no compiler flags stated; the 'Go NATS' baseline's configuration (defaults vs tuned) is not detailed; very low star count relative to HN traction suggests little independent verification
found_via: Hacker News: 'Show HN: BusterMQ, Thread-per-core NATS server in Zig with io_uring' (https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=46449812), query 'thread-per-core io_uring'

name: gnet
baseline: Go net/http standard library (epoll-based netpoller); direct epoll on Linux, kqueue on macOS
workload: Echo-server throughput/latency sweep across 1,000-10,000 TCP connections and 512B-64KB packet sizes on Linux (epoll) and macOS (kqueue), comparing gnet vs Go std net, evio, and netpoll (gnet-io/gnet-benchmarks: echo-gnet-server vs echo-net-server vs echo-evio-server vs echo-netpoll-server)
claimed_speedup: gnet ranked #1 of 486 frameworks (all languages) in TechEmpower Round 22 plaintext; separately shown outperforming echo-net-server (std net), echo-evio-server, and echo-netpoll-server across the connection/packet-size sweep (charted as images, no single numeric ratio stated in text)
compiler_and_flags: Go 1.17.2 (Linux run) / Go 1.16.5 (macOS run); default build flags, not further specified
hardware: Linux run: Ubuntu 20.04, 8-core AMD EPYC 7K62, 16GB RAM; macOS run: 6-core Intel i7-9750H, 16GB RAM; TechEmpower run: 28 HT-core Intel Xeon Gold 5120, 32GB RAM
stars_or_usage: 11.3k stars; used in production at ByteDance and others per repo's user list
tradeoffs: Event-driven single-goroutine-per-loop model trades away Go's simple goroutine-per-connection model; author notes the TechEmpower HTTP implementation is 'half-baked ... far from production-ready'
caveats: Benchmark numbers are presented as chart images, not tabulated figures, so exact ratios can't be quoted verbatim; build flags not stated; TechEmpower ranking mixes many frameworks/languages rather than a clean 1:1 baseline comparison
found_via: Hacker News: 'Gnet: A high-performance, event-loop networking library written in pure Go' (https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=21078091), query 'event loop library'

name: Hinsightd MT (hin10)
workload: Concurrent-connection sweep (c=50..1000) serving a 102-byte index.html and an 89.7kB jquery.js, sendfile disabled on all servers, 4-core machine; hinsightd 0.10.1 (io_uring, falls back to epoll) vs nginx 1.25.3, lighttpd 1.4.72, Apache 2.4.58, caddy 2.7.5
claimed_speedup: index.html at c=50: hinsightd/0.10.1 127,296 req/s vs nginx 117,020 req/s (~1.09x); at c=1000: 77,152 vs 76,079 req/s (~1.01x); jquery.js (no sendfile) at c=50: hinsightd 28,277 vs nginx 36,029 req/s (hinsightd slower on this workload)
hardware: 4-core machine, no hyperthreading (CPU model not stated)
tradeoffs: No sendfile support in this test; wins only on the tiny static file and only by a small margin (1-9%); loses to nginx on the larger jquery.js payload; author states the branch 'still needs some optimization and testing'
caveats: Author's own blog benchmark; no CPU model, compiler, or build flags stated; margin over nginx is small and workload-dependent; repo has no LICENSE file
found_via: Hacker News: 'Hinsightd a multi-threaded io_uring web server: benchmarks' (https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=38302070), query 'io_uring benchmark'

name: rsloop
workload: asyncio-compatible event loop microbenchmarks (200K callbacks, 50K tasks, 5,000 TCP roundtrips) plus a sustained network workload matrix (HTTP keep-alive, TLS, WebSockets, bulk transfer) and idle-activation latency; rsloop vs stdlib asyncio, uvloop, and zuvloop
claimed_speedup: 5,000 TCP roundtrips: rsloop 83.30ms vs uvloop 127.87ms (~1.53x faster); TLS HTTP throughput: rsloop 72,496 rps vs uvloop 26,226 rps (~2.76x); bulk transfer: rsloop 2,009.9 MiB/s vs uvloop 1,264.9 MiB/s (~1.59x); idle-activation first-reply latency: rsloop 17.221ms vs uvloop 18.193ms. Not a universal win: uvloop/zuvloop beat rsloop on plaintext callbacks, tasks, and some WebSocket scenarios
compiler_and_flags: rsloop built in Rust release mode (cargo --release); CPython 3.14.7; uvloop 0.22.1
tradeoffs: Results are workload-dependent: rsloop leads TCP/TLS/bulk-transfer scenarios but loses to uvloop/zuvloop on raw callback/task scheduling and some WebSocket scenarios; author explicitly cautions these are local microbenchmarks, not isolated-lab or general application performance claims; trades helper-thread CPU for loop-thread work under contention
caveats: First-party benchmark (same author wrote rsloop and the harness) but unusually rigorous: pinned dependency versions, medians of 7 runs with warmups, fresh subprocesses, confidence intervals for idle-latency; exact rustc version/flags beyond 'release mode' not given
found_via: Hacker News: 'Show HN: An event loop for asyncio written in Rust' (https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=47472041), query 'Show HN event loop'

name: PhotonLibOS io_uring vs epoll echo-server comparison
workload: Coroutine-based echo server (ping-pong and streaming/multiplexed client modes), single-connection QPS/throughput at buffer sizes 64B-16KB, PhotonLibOS's io_uring backend vs its epoll backend, on 2 cloud VMs
claimed_speedup: Streaming mode, buf=64B: epoll 1,565K qps / 780Mb/s vs io_uring 506K qps / 260Mb/s (epoll ~3.1x faster); buf=16384B: epoll 224K qps / 27.3Gb/s vs io_uring 183K qps / 22.5Gb/s (epoll ~1.2x faster). Author separately states io_uring 'can always surpass' epoll in ping-pong-mode workloads, but gives no numbers for that case in this thread
hardware: 2x Intel Xeon Platinum 8369B @2.70GHz cloud VMs, 96 cores/128GB RAM, 40Gb network, CentOS 8, kernel 6.0.7
tradeoffs: Result is workload-shape-dependent: io_uring wins ping-pong (single round-trip) workloads but loses to epoll in streaming/multiplexed (IO-depth=1) workloads in this test; the gap narrows as buffer size grows; author also found plain psync 3-4x faster than io_uring for pure in-memory (tmpfs) IO at IO depth 1
caveats: This is a negative/mixed result for io_uring vs epoll in streaming mode specifically -- included as evidence for the already-catalogued PhotonLibOS entry, not as a new 'faster than epoll' candidate; no compiler/build flags stated; the ping-pong-mode numbers (where io_uring reportedly wins) are not shown in this thread
found_via: Hacker News: 'A performance review of io_uring vs. epoll for standard/streamed socket traffic' (https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=33492267), query 'io_uring vs epoll'
